title: Transactions & Concurrency
subtitle: ACID, transaction control, anomalies, locks, 2PL, serializability and deadlock — exam-oriented practice.
source: BankSoIt DBMS Production Deck — Module 06. Questions are independently crafted from the module topics for competitive-exam practice.
instructions: Choose one answer for each question.
Questions are designed for IBPS SO IT, RRB Scale II IT, SBI SO and similar Computer Science/IT examinations.
Review the explanation, important point, exam trap and hint after submission.
description: ACID, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, concurrency anomalies, locks, 2PL, serializability and deadlock.

questions.question: A transaction transfers ₹500 from Account A to Account B. The debit succeeds but the credit fails, and the system leaves the database with only the debit. Which ACID property has been violated?
questions.explanation: The transfer should occur as an all-or-nothing unit; leaving only the debit means the transaction was partially applied.
questions.importantPoint: Atomicity means all operations of a transaction occur or none do.
questions.examTrap: Durability concerns committed results surviving failures; isolation concerns concurrent transactions.
questions.hint: Use the “all or nothing” test.

questions.question: Which ACID property requires a committed transaction’s effects to survive a subsequent system crash?
questions.explanation: Durability requires committed changes to persist despite failures.
questions.importantPoint: Durability = committed effects survive failures.
questions.examTrap: Atomicity is all-or-nothing; isolation controls interaction among concurrent transactions.
questions.hint: Think about what must remain after a crash.

questions.question: A transaction temporarily produces an invalid database state but completes with all integrity constraints satisfied. Which ACID property is concerned with preserving valid states from one committed state to another?
questions.explanation: Consistency requires a transaction to take the database from one valid state to another valid state, subject to constraints.
questions.importantPoint: Consistency preserves database rules and integrity constraints.
questions.examTrap: Isolation is about concurrent execution, not the validity of the committed state itself.
questions.hint: Focus on database rules remaining satisfied.

questions.question: Which command makes the changes of the current transaction permanent?
questions.explanation: COMMIT ends the transaction successfully and makes its changes permanent according to the DBMS transaction model.
questions.importantPoint: COMMIT makes transaction changes permanent.
questions.examTrap: ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted work; SAVEPOINT creates an intermediate rollback point.
questions.hint: Which command signals successful completion of the transaction?

questions.question: A transaction updates several rows and then executes ROLLBACK before COMMIT. What is the normal effect on those uncommitted changes?

options.text: They are converted into a savepoint
They are copied into the log only

questions.explanation: ROLLBACK reverses the transaction’s uncommitted work.
questions.importantPoint: ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted transaction changes.
questions.examTrap: COMMIT, not ROLLBACK, makes changes permanent.
questions.hint: Think about the purpose of rollback in transaction control.

questions.question: Which statement best describes SAVEPOINT?

options.text: It creates a point within a transaction to which partial rollback can be performed
It starts a new database instance
It automatically releases all locks immediately

questions.explanation: SAVEPOINT marks an intermediate point so a transaction can roll back part of its work without necessarily discarding all earlier work.
questions.importantPoint: SAVEPOINT supports partial rollback within a transaction.
questions.examTrap: It is not a substitute for COMMIT and does not itself start a new database instance.
questions.hint: Think of SAVEPOINT as an intermediate recovery position within one transaction.

questions.question: Transaction T2 reads a value written by T1 before T1 commits. T1 later rolls back. What anomaly did T2 experience?
questions.explanation: T2 consumed uncommitted data from T1, which later disappeared due to rollback; this is a dirty read.
questions.importantPoint: Dirty read = reading uncommitted data.
questions.examTrap: A lost update involves overwriting another transaction’s update; a phantom concerns a changing set of rows.
questions.hint: Was the value read committed at the time it was read?

questions.question: T1 reads the same row twice and gets different committed values because T2 updates and commits that row between the two reads. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: The same row is read twice and returns different values due to another committed update, which is a non-repeatable read.
questions.importantPoint: Non-repeatable read concerns the value of the same row changing between reads.
questions.examTrap: A phantom read concerns newly appearing/disappearing rows in a result set.
questions.hint: Focus on one existing row being read twice.

questions.question: T1 executes a query returning all employees in Dept 10. T2 inserts another Dept 10 employee and commits. T1 repeats the query and gets an additional row. Which anomaly is illustrated?
questions.explanation: A phantom read occurs when a repeated range/set query sees a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or removed qualifying rows.
questions.importantPoint: Phantom = changed set of rows for the same predicate.
questions.examTrap: Non-repeatable read is typically framed around a changed value of an existing row.
questions.hint: Ask whether the row set itself changed.

questions.question: Which lock is normally required when a transaction intends to modify a data item?
questions.explanation: An exclusive lock provides write access while preventing conflicting access according to the locking protocol.
questions.importantPoint: Exclusive lock is associated with writing/updating.
questions.examTrap: A shared lock is primarily associated with reading and can be compatible with other shared locks.
questions.hint: Match the lock type with a write operation.

questions.question: Two transactions both hold shared locks on a row and both need to convert them to exclusive locks. Which problem can arise because each waits for the other to release its shared lock?
questions.explanation: Each transaction can wait for the other, producing a cycle in the wait-for relationship: a deadlock.
questions.importantPoint: Deadlock can arise from circular waiting for locks.
questions.examTrap: Dirty reads and checkpoints are unrelated to this lock-conversion cycle.
questions.hint: Look for mutual waiting.

questions.question: In the growing phase of two-phase locking (2PL), a transaction may:

options.text: Release locks but never acquire new ones
Acquire locks but not release them

questions.explanation: During the growing phase, locks may be acquired but none are released; releases occur in the shrinking phase.
questions.importantPoint: 2PL: growing = acquire; shrinking = release.
questions.examTrap: The protocol does not restrict the growing phase to shared locks only.
questions.hint: Recall the two phases as acquire first, release later.

questions.question: Under basic two-phase locking, once a transaction releases its first lock, what is it prohibited from doing?
questions.explanation: After the first lock release, the transaction is in the shrinking phase and cannot acquire new locks.
questions.importantPoint: The key 2PL boundary is that no new lock is acquired after the first release.
questions.examTrap: The transaction can still perform other operations subject to the protocol; the specific restriction is on acquiring locks.
questions.hint: Identify the action that changes the phase from growing to shrinking.

questions.question: A schedule is conflict-serializable if its precedence graph is:
questions.explanation: A schedule is conflict-serializable exactly when its precedence graph has no cycle.
questions.importantPoint: Acyclic precedence graph → conflict-serializable schedule.
questions.examTrap: A cycle indicates that no equivalent serial order exists under conflict-serializability.
questions.hint: Look for the graph property used to test conflict serializability.

questions.question: Consider the schedule: T1 reads X, T2 writes X, T1 writes X. The conflicting operations create which relationship from T2 to T1?

options.text: T2 → T1 because T2’s write precedes T1’s write on X
T1 → T2 because T1 reads before T2 writes
No edge can exist because both transactions access X

questions.explanation: T2’s write on X occurs before T1’s write on X, and the operations conflict, so the precedence graph contains T2 → T1.
questions.importantPoint: A write-write conflict creates an edge from the earlier transaction to the later one.
questions.examTrap: The direction follows the order of the conflicting operations in the schedule.
questions.hint: Compare the order of the conflicting writes.

questions.question: Which set of conditions is classically associated with the possibility of deadlock?

options.text: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait

questions.explanation: The classic necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.
questions.importantPoint: Deadlock conditions describe how transactions can become permanently blocked by one another.
questions.examTrap: ACID properties are not deadlock conditions.
questions.hint: Recall the four Coffman conditions.

questions.question: If a transaction holds a shared lock on item X, which access is generally compatible with that lock under a basic lock-compatibility model?

options.text: Another transaction acquiring a shared lock on X
Another transaction acquiring an exclusive lock on X
Another transaction deleting X while ignoring locks
Any operation regardless of lock type

questions.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks because both represent read access.
questions.importantPoint: S-S is compatible; S-X is not.
questions.examTrap: Compatibility depends on the lock matrix, not on ignoring locks.
questions.hint: Think about multiple readers versus a writer.

questions.question: Which statement best describes isolation in ACID?

options.text: Concurrent transactions should behave as if their intermediate effects are appropriately controlled
Every transaction must use a foreign key
A transaction must always execute faster than other transactions

questions.explanation: Isolation controls how concurrent transactions interact so intermediate effects do not improperly interfere.
questions.importantPoint: Isolation concerns concurrent execution behavior.
questions.examTrap: Durability, not isolation, concerns survival of committed data after failures.
questions.hint: Focus on concurrent transactions interacting with each other.

questions.question: A schedule executes all operations of T1 before all operations of T2. What kind of schedule is this?
questions.explanation: A serial schedule completes one transaction before beginning the next, so no interleaving occurs.
questions.importantPoint: Serial = transactions execute one after another without interleaving.
questions.examTrap: Recoverability is a different property and is not guaranteed merely by the label “serial” in every broader sense.
questions.hint: Ask whether operations of the transactions are interleaved.

questions.question: Which statement about deadlock detection is correct?

options.text: A cycle in a wait-for graph can indicate deadlock
A cycle always means the database has achieved serializability
A wait-for graph cannot represent transaction waiting

questions.explanation: A cycle in the wait-for graph indicates circular waiting, which is the signature of a deadlock among the involved transactions.
questions.importantPoint: Wait-for graph cycles are used to detect deadlock.
questions.examTrap: Serializability and deadlock are different concepts.
questions.hint: Look for circular waiting between transactions.
